playground.label: Project 5: back up a folder into numbered ZIP files (temporary folder, no input)
playground.code:
import os, shutil, tempfile, zipfile
from pathlib import Path

root = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
spam = root / 'spam'
(spam / 'eggs').mkdir(parents=True)
(spam / 'file1.txt').write_text('Hello')
(spam / 'eggs' / 'file2.txt').write_text('Hello' * 100)
os.chdir(root)

def backup_to_zip(folder):
    folder = Path(folder)
    number = 1
    while True:
        zip_filename = Path(folder.parts[-1] + '_' + str(number) + '.zip')
        if not zip_filename.exists():
            break
        number = number + 1
    print(f'Creating {zip_filename}...')
    with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_filename, 'w', zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as backup_zip:
        for folder_name, subfolders, filenames in os.walk(folder):
            subfolders.sort()
            filenames.sort()
            folder_name = Path(folder_name)
            print(f'Adding files in folder {folder_name.relative_to(root)}...')
            for filename in filenames:
                print(f'Adding file {filename}...')
                path = folder_name / filename
                backup_zip.write(path, arcname=path.relative_to(root))
    print('Done.')

backup_to_zip(spam)
backup_to_zip(spam)
print(sorted(zipfile.ZipFile('spam_2.zip').namelist()))
os.chdir('/')
shutil.rmtree(root)

findings: Chapter 11 of the 3rd edition, Organizing Files, teaches the shutil module with shutil.copy(), shutil.copytree() and shutil.move() for copying, moving and renaming; permanent deletion with os.unlink(), os.rmdir() and shutil.rmtree(), with a dry run as protection and the third-party send2trash module as the recoverable alternative; listing a folder with os.listdir() and iterdir() and walking a tree with os.walk(), shown by a program that renames every file to upper case; the zipfile module, with ZipFile objects in write, append and read use, namelist(), getinfo() with file_size and compress_size, extractall() and extract(); Project 5, backup_to_zip.py, which writes a folder into a ZIP file whose name counts up; and it closes with a summary, 4 practice questions and 4 practice programs: selective copying, finding large files, renumbering files and converting American to European dates.

The chapter's printed outputs reproduce under Python 3.14.4 except one sentence: shutil.copy() returned a str when the destination was a folder and a PosixPath when it was a file name, which is what the chapter prints; the walk of the chapter gave the same folders and files on each pass, but the documentation says that the order of names depends on the file system, so the chapter's listing is one possible order and the runs here sorted the names; the ZIP listing reproduced the member name file1.txt, file_size 50000, compress_size 97 and Compressed file is 515.46x smaller!, while the chapter's prose puts the compressed size at about 213 bytes, a number that neither compresslevel 9 nor the default level 6 gave (both 97; level 1 gave 293 and level 0 gave 50010), so the prose and the listing disagree with each other and only the listing runs.

The chapter says that a file1.txt already in the destination folder of shutil.move() would be overwritten; under Python 3.14.4 shutil.move() into a folder that already held file1.txt raised shutil.Error and moved nothing, which is what the documentation states (the destination path in the folder must not already exist), whereas a move onto an existing path that is not a folder replaced the file; the chapter also describes the return value of shutil.move() as a string, and it was a str for a folder destination and a PosixPath for a new file name.

The chapter's Project 5 program differs from what its prose intends in four ways that were run: write() without a compression type stores the file, so the snapshot is not compressed although the chapter speaks of compressing; passing absolute paths to write() stores the whole path of each file without its leading slash as the member name; giving the folder as Path('.') raises IndexError, because Path('.').parts is an empty tuple; and when the archive is created inside the folder being backed up, os.walk lists the archive and the program writes it into itself; the program also tests names in the working directory and not next to the folder.

The chapter's advice on deletion holds: os.unlink() deletes a file for good, os.rmdir() only an empty folder (OSError otherwise) and shutil.rmtree() a whole tree, and the dry run, in which the delete is replaced by a print, exposed the typo *.rxt for *.txt by matching no file; current Python adds that unlink() on a folder raises IsADirectoryError on this Linux system, that rmtree() on a missing path raises FileNotFoundError unless ignore_errors=True, and that the onexc parameter, added in Python 3.12, replaces the deprecated onerror as the way to handle errors while deleting a tree; send2trash was not executed.

For an advanced course, chapter 11 is best taught by asking of each operation whether it can be undone, whether it stays inside the folder it was given, and whether the program can show what it will do before it does it: copy and copytree keep the source and move does not, rmtree, unlink and rmdir cannot be undone and send2trash can; the chapter's outputs hold under 3.14.4 except the overwrite claim for shutil.move and the 213-byte sentence, and Project 5 needs its compression type, its archive names, its folder argument and the place of its archive fixed, while pathlib's walk, copy and move, the exclusive and append modes, make_archive and the safety of extraction are what the chapter leaves for the course to add.

Current Python gives file handling more than the chapter presents: shutil.copy2() keeps metadata such as the modification time and copytree() uses it, copytree(dirs_exist_ok=True) copies into an existing folder, Path objects are accepted by the shutil and os functions since PEP 519 and have iterdir(), glob() and rglob(), Path.walk() since Python 3.12 is os.walk() for Path objects, and since Python 3.14 Path.copy(), copy_into(), move() and move_into() copy and move without shutil.

Current Python gives archives more than the chapter presents: ZipFile mode 'x' refuses to overwrite and 'a' adds, ZipFile.mkdir() since Python 3.11 adds a folder entry, compression methods beyond deflate include ZIP_BZIP2, ZIP_LZMA and, new in Python 3.14, ZIP_ZSTANDARD, shutil.make_archive() and shutil.unpack_archive() do in one call what the chapter does with a program, extraction removes .. and leading slashes from member names so that the members of a hostile archive stay inside the target folder, and the documentation still warns never to extract untrusted archives without inspection.

nodes.label: Copying and moving
nodes.body: Copying, moving and renaming files and folders with the shutil module is the first subject of Chapter 11 (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Copying
nodes.body: Two functions copy: shutil.copy for one file and shutil.copytree for a folder with everything in it (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Copy file
nodes.body: shutil.copy(source, destination) copies a file to a folder, which keeps the name, or to a file name, which becomes the copy's name (Sweigart, 2025); in a run under Python 3.14.4 copying a.txt into a folder and to b.txt in it left both a.txt and b.txt there, and the documentation adds that an existing destination file is replaced, that permission bits are copied and that other metadata is not (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: shutil.copy copies one file to a destination that is either a folder, which keeps the file's name, or a file name, which becomes the copy's name; an existing destination file is replaced, and the call returns the path of the new file.

nodes.label: Copy with metadata
nodes.body: shutil.copy2 is not in the chapter; it copies as shutil.copy does and also tries to keep metadata such as the modification time, so a file whose time was set to 1000000000 kept it in a copy2 copy and did not in a copy made by shutil.copy, and copytree copies its files with copy2 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: shutil.copy2 copies a file like shutil.copy and also tries to keep its metadata, such as the modification time, which shutil.copy does not keep; copytree uses copy2 for every file.

nodes.body: The chapter's copytree needs a destination that does not exist (Sweigart, 2025); since Python 3.8 dirs_exist_ok=True lets it continue into an existing folder, where a file of the same name is overwritten and other files stay, so with a.txt changed from 'old' to 'new' the folder held a.txt and keep.txt (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: With dirs_exist_ok=True, copytree continues into a destination folder that already exists and overwrites files of the same name there, leaving the other files in place.

nodes.label: Moving
nodes.body: shutil.move moves and renames, and the chapter treats the two as one operation (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Move file or folder
nodes.body: shutil.move(h / 'spam/file1.txt', h / 'spam2') moves the file into the folder and keeps its name (Sweigart, 2025); the chapter says it returns a string, and in a run under 3.14.4 it returned a str when the destination was a folder and a PosixPath when it was a new file name, the same as shutil.copy does; across file systems the function copies and then deletes (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: shutil.move moves a file or a folder to a destination and returns where it went; if the destination is an existing folder the source goes inside it under its own name, and across file systems the move is a copy followed by a delete.

nodes.label: Pathlib copy move
nodes.body: The chapter uses shutil for all copying and moving (Sweigart, 2025); Python 3.14 added Path.copy, Path.copy_into, Path.move and Path.move_into, and under 3.14.4 copy returned a Path and left the original in place, move left the old name missing, and copy_into and move_into put the file into an existing folder under its own name (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Since Python 3.14 a Path object can copy and move itself with Path.copy, Path.copy_into, Path.move and Path.move_into, and they return the new Path; before 3.14 this needed shutil, so the page of this course runs these only under 3.14.

nodes.body: Deleting is where the chapter warns most, and its answer is the dry run and the recycle bin (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Permanent deletion

nodes.label: Safer deletion
nodes.body: The chapter offers two protections against a bug that deletes the wrong files: a dry run and the recycle bin (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Dry run
nodes.body: The chapter's program with the typo glob('*.rxt') would delete .rxt files, and a version with the delete commented out and a print added shows it (Sweigart, 2025); run on a folder holding a.txt and b.txt, the .rxt pattern matched 0 files and so printed nothing, where the pattern *.txt would have printed a.txt and b.txt, which is how the dry run exposes the typo; the chapter advises dry runs for copy, rename and move as well (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.body: The chapter shows one order of output (Sweigart, 2025); the documentation says that the order of names depends on the file system, that a folder comes before its subfolders by default and that topdown=False turns this around, which a test on a folder a with a subfolder b gave as ., a, a/b top-down and a/b, a, . bottom-up; bottom-up is the order in which rmdir can empty a tree, as the documentation's own rmtree example does (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: By default os.walk gives a folder before its subfolders; with topdown=False it gives the subfolders first, which is the order needed to delete a tree with rmdir, and the order of names inside one folder depends on the file system.

nodes.label: Compression method
nodes.body: write compresses only when compress_type=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED is passed; without it the file is stored at its regular size (Sweigart, 2025); under 3.14.4 ZIP_STORED is 0 and ZIP_DEFLATED is 8, the stored member of 50000 bytes stayed 50000 bytes and the deflated one was smaller, and ZIP_BZIP2, ZIP_LZMA and ZIP_ZSTANDARD are 12, 14 and 93, the last one new in Python 3.14 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The compression method is ZIP_STORED by default, which does not compress at all, or ZIP_DEFLATED, which the chapter recommends; the standard library also offers ZIP_BZIP2 and ZIP_LZMA, and ZIP_ZSTANDARD since Python 3.14.

nodes.body: The second program prints files larger than 100MB with os.path.getsize (Sweigart, 2025); a solution written for this study used 100 * 1024 * 1024 bytes as the limit, created sparse files of 100 MB and 100 MB plus one byte, and printed only the second, 104857601 bytes; the same code with a limit of 1000 bytes is the example of this concept, where the chapter does not say whether MB means 10^6 or 2^20 bytes (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The second practice program walks a tree and prints the files whose size from os.path.getsize exceeds a limit; the chapter's limit is 100MB, and the same code is shown here with a limit of 1000 bytes on small test files.

nodes.label: Renumber files
nodes.body: The third program closes gaps in numbered file names, with the chapter's 117 files spam001.txt to spam120.txt missing 42, 86 and 103 (Sweigart, 2025); a solution written for this study renamed each file to the next number in sorted order, and the result was spam001.txt to spam117.txt with no gap, spam042.txt being the old spam043.txt; the added challenge of inserting a gap was not built (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The third practice program finds the numbered files of a prefix, locates gaps in the numbers and renames the later files down to close them; str.zfill pads a number with zeros to the width of the names.

io.code:
(lambda g: exec('import os, shutil, tempfile, zipfile, io
from pathlib import Path
t = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
for i in (1, 2, 4, 5, n):
    (t/('spam%s.txt' % str(i).zfill(3))).write_text('')
files = sorted(p for p in t.iterdir() if p.name.startswith('spam'))
for new_number, p in enumerate(files, start=1):
    new_name = 'spam%s.txt' % str(new_number).zfill(3)
    if p.name != new_name:
        shutil.move(p, p.with_name(new_name))
out = sorted(p.name for p in t.iterdir())
shutil.rmtree(t)

nodes.label: Date renaming
nodes.body: The fourth program swaps the month and the day in names with MM-DD-YYYY dates (Sweigart, 2025); a solution written for this study walked a folder, matched (\d\d)-(\d\d)-(\d\d\d\d) and used re.sub with the groups in the order 2, 1, 3, which turned spam12-31-1900.txt into spam31-12-1900.txt and report01-02-2020.txt into report02-01-2020.txt and left notes.txt alone (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The fourth practice program finds file names with an American date MM-DD-YYYY and renames them to the European DD-MM-YYYY by swapping the first two groups of a regular expression, using shutil.move to rename; a name without a date is left alone.

io.code:
(lambda g: (exec('import os, shutil, tempfile, zipfile, io
from pathlib import Path
t = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
import re
for n in ('spam12-31-1900.txt', 'report01-02-2020.txt', 'notes.txt'):
    (t/n).write_text('')
pattern = re.compile(r'(\d\d)-(\d\d)-(\d\d\d\d)')
for folder_name, subfolders, filenames in os.walk(t):
    for filename in filenames:
        if pattern.search(filename):
            shutil.move(Path(folder_name) / filename, Path(folder_name) / pattern.sub(r'\2-\1-\3', filename))
out = sorted(p.name for p in t.iterdir())
shutil.rmtree(t)
', g), g['out'])[1])({})
